rewrites.summary:
Tennessee is the only state in the country with a standing criminal ban on gender-expressive performance: the Adult Entertainment Act (2023) criminalises 'adult cabaret entertainment' — defined to include 'male or female impersonators' — anywhere a child could see it, at up to 11 months 29 days and a $2,500 fine for a first offence and a 1–6 year felony on repeat. The ban is enforceable and current: the appeals court revived it on standing grounds and the Supreme Court declined review (February 2025), so a visitor presenting in drag faces live charging exposure today rather than a dead-letter law.

For practical safety, killings of trans women run at 7.8 per 100k per year — above the general national homicide rate.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Adjacent litigation and policy flux: the Supreme Court upheld the state's ban on gender-affirming care for minors in June 2025, and the drag ban's constitutionality has never been decided on the merits. A civil-liberties suit over a district attorney's threat to charge a 2023 Pride event also remains ongoing.
rewrites.localsOnly: Since 2026 the state has also mandated birth-sex placement in prisons and shelters — a resident-facing facility practice.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: No drag-ban prosecutions are publicly reported, so actual charging practice is unverified. The killing-rate figure rests on 10 recorded deaths (2008–2025), treated as an undercount floor.

rewrites.summary: Kansas's SB 244 (signed February 2026) is among the harshest instruments a traveller can meet: it confines trans people to birth-sex facilities in government buildings and voids state-issued IDs with corrected markers — licences invalid from 26 February 2026, no grace period, holders notified. The law also creates a private right of action under which anyone may sue a person they suspect of a violation for about $1,000 — a bounty-style exposure that the February 2026 legal-risk assessment singled out as the cycle's first 'Do Not Travel' addition, warning it 'could meaningfully affect interstate travel'.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Two trans men sued within days of enactment (Doe v. State of Kansas, with civil-liberties counsel), citing fear of violence under the law; a May 2026 injunction covers only the healthcare provisions, leaving the facility and ID regime in force.
rewrites.localsOnly: The ID invalidation operates through holder records: the state's revenue agency has been mailing written notice, and many holders have already been told their licences are now invalid.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: The underlying news report on the lawsuit was not retrievable at fetch time, so its claims rest on the source summary. Whether the $1,000 private right of action has produced any actual suits is not reported.

rewrites.summary: The February 2026 and July 2026 legal-risk assessments rank Indiana among the harshest anti-trans states in the country, citing its 2026 identity-document law — from 1 February 2026 the driver's-licence and ID bureaus no longer change gender markers — and escalating bathroom restrictions as the drivers of its adult-risk rating.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Judicial and legislative flux: in May 2023 the state's highest court declined, in split votes, to hear two cases of transgender girls seeking gender changes on birth certificates, leaving rulings that trial courts lack authority to grant such changes absent legislation; and in January 2026 the state Senate approved a bill (37-8) that would define sex and gender, ban birth-certificate amendments, restrict bathrooms in public schools and restrict housing in prisons.
rewrites.localsOnly: The 2026 ID rule ends the long-standing route of obtaining a gender-marker change through a court-ordered gender change or physician statement, and advocates who testified warned it will forcibly out transgender and nonbinary residents.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: SB 182 was sent to the House after the 27 January 2026 Senate vote; whether it became law is unresolved in the record. The identity-document ban took effect as an administrative rule change on 1 February 2026.

News reporting: from 1 February 2026, residents lost the option to change their gender marker on driver's licences or other identification cards when the motor-vehicle bureau's new ban took effect, ending a long-standing court-ordered or physician-statement route; advocates who testified warned it will forcibly out transgender and nonbinary residents; a pending bill would create legal definitions for sex and gender, ban birth-certificate amendments, restrict bathrooms in public schools and restrict housing in prisons.

News reporting (January 2026): the state/province Senate approved a bill (37-8, party-line) requiring public K-12 schools and public universities to designate multi-person restrooms, locker rooms and changing areas for use only by males or females based on reproductive biology at birth, barring transgender students from facilities matching their gender identity; opponents argued that letting anyone directly or indirectly injured sue a school would encourage harassment-style enforcement.

News reporting (May 2023): the highest court of the state/province declined, in split votes, to hear two cases of transgender girls seeking to change the gender on their birth certificates, leaving appeals-court rulings standing that trial courts lack authority to grant such changes unless the legislature codifies them; one case involved a nine-year-old transgender girl whose birth certificate's male designation allowed her school to restrict her bathroom access.
rewrites.notes: ID-document and adult-risk exposure in summary; birth-certificate litigation and pending bill in tangential; resident document-route impact in localsOnly.

rewrites.summary: A 2025 facility ban — signed 21 March 2025, effective 1 July 2025 — restricts bathrooms, locker rooms and changing areas in public schools and state-owned buildings to sex assigned at birth, the first anti-trans bathroom law in the state's history. The July 2026 legal-risk assessment places the state in the worst-law group.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: The record rates the state below the national score of 0.36; the ban's enactment followed repeated legislative failures (2016, 2017, twice in 2018 and 2022), marking a policy reversal rather than a settled trajectory.
rewrites.localsOnly: The measure primarily targets K-12 schools and state colleges, including off-campus activities, and covers state-run facilities generally; a 'reasonable accommodation' clause raised the prospect during floor debate that incarcerated trans people would be placed in solitary confinement.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: The facility ban's effective date (1 July 2025) and the solitary-confinement prospect for incarcerated people are documented through news reports; the record holds no implementation or enforcement data.
